item.research_question: Is it feasible to produce the refractory metal high entropy alloy W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 via laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) using in-situ alloy formation from elemental powders, and how do process parameters influence microstructure, defects, and mechanical properties?
item.material_system: W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 refractory metal high entropy alloy (50 at% V, 20 at% W, 20 at% Mo, 20 at% Ta, 20 at% Nb in initial mix with 1.5x V compensation)
item.processing_route: Laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) using an AconityMINI machine with a 1 kW fiber laser (1080 nm, 70 µm beam diameter) on Mo substrates; two parameter sets tested: Set A (600 W, 800 mm/s, 120 µm hatch) and Set B (100 W, 100 mm/s, 45 µm hatch); volumetric energy densities of 125 J/mm³ and 889 J/mm³ respectively; argon shielding gas with <25 ppm O2
item.test_conditions: Samples built as 6 × 6 × 6 mm³ cubes; analyzed via SEM, EBSD, TEM, EDS, and microhardness testing; relative density measured by optical microscopy; microhardness measured at HV0.1 load
key_findings: Relative densities reached 99.8% for parameter set A and 99.5% for parameter set B.
A single bcc-phase was confirmed by EBSD, consistent with vacuum arc melted samples.
Average grain size was 16.3 µm for PBF-LB/M B, which is more than four times smaller than the 80 µm reported for vacuum arc melted samples.
Parameter set A produced coarser dendritic structures with secondary dendrites, while set B produced an almost cellular structure.
Microhardness was 561 ± 17 HV0.1 for the coarser structure (Set A) and 614 ± 21 HV0.1 for the finer cellular structure (Set B).
Vanadium was concentrated in interdendritic areas, while W and Ta were predominantly located in intradendritic areas.
Parameter set B (lower scan speed, higher energy density) resulted in fewer undissolved W particles compared to Set A.
Cracks were observed in both sets, with wider cracks in Set B attributed to higher volumetric energy density and smaller hatch distance.
item.mechanism: The high cooling rates (~10^6 K/s) in PBF-LB/M mitigate elemental segregation and refine grain size compared to conventional melting. The solidification mode (dendritic vs. cellular) is controlled by the ratio of growth rate (R) and temperature gradient (G), where higher R and lower G favor dendrites (Set A) and lower R and higher G favor cellular structures (Set B). Cracking is caused by internal stresses from the thermal gradient combined with the alloy's low room temperature ductility and embrittlement at grain boundaries due to O and N impurities. Undissolved W particles are reduced by higher volumetric energy input and slower scan speeds, which increase interaction time and re-melting.
item.limitations: Samples still contained cracks and undissolved tungsten particles; the alloy exhibits low room temperature ductility leading to hot cracking and stress-induced cracking; the study did not achieve completely defect-free samples.
item.future_work: Verification of crack-free processing using high-temperature build-platform heating (>600 °C) or high-purity powders with low O and N content; investigation of more recently developed refractory metal high entropy alloys with increased room temperature ductility (e.g., Al10Nb15Ta5Ti30Zr40) to enable crack-free processing without heating.
quotes: The relative density of the samples with a dimension of 6 × 6 × 6 mm 3 reaches, in dependence of the PBF-LB/M parameter set, 99.8%.
The average grain size determined by the linear intercept method is 16.3 µm. This is more than a factor of four smaller than the 80 µm reported by Senkov et al. for vacuum arc molten samples.
The microhardness of the PBF-LB/M A sample with the coarser structure is 561 ± 17 HV0.1 (n = 9) while the microhardness of the PBF-LB/M B sample is 614 ± 21 HV0.1 (n = 9).
